commit_scope: working tree as mounted, dev/staging/main reported identical at 30dcc9a as of early July 2026 per project memory; not independently re-verified against git log in this pass
methodology: Direct reading of api/*.py (all 12 deployed route files + 2 orphaned files), schema.sql, all migration-*.sql files, vercel.json, requirements.txt, .github/workflows/tests.yml, tests/run-tests.mjs, .env.example, targeted grep of index.html (4471 lines); pip-audit run against requirements.txt pins; cross-checked against two pre-existing internal audit documents (multi-tenant-audit-report.txt dated 2026-07-14, sysconic-code-and-architecture-audit.md, undated) with independent re-verification of their claims against current code rather than taking them on faith.

findings.title: No Row-Level Security on core tenant tables; RLS exists only on Project Performance module tables
findings.business_impact: A single missed `.eq('company_id', ...)` filter in any current or future backend route is a direct, database-permitted cross-tenant data read/write with zero database-layer backstop, for every core business table (companies, users, invites, quotes, quote_versions, quote_version_reviewers, quote_emails, quote_activity, vendors, products, customers, company_integrations, projects).
findings.technical_risk: Tenant isolation for the entire application is enforced 100% in Python application code. All 12 deployed api/*.py files connect via SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY (service-role), which bypasses RLS unconditionally even where RLS is enabled. RLS was enabled for the 21 tables added in migration-project-performance.sql (purchase orders, bills, invoices, baselines, alerts, etc.) but was never retrofitted onto the original schema.sql tables or onto customers/company_integrations/projects, which were added via untracked/manual migrations.
findings.evidence: schema.sql (no `enable row level security` or `create policy` statements anywhere); migration-project-performance.sql:449-482 (RLS enabled + `tenant_isolation` policy created only for a specific list of 21 table names); every api/*.py does `SUPABASE_KEY = os.environ.get('SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY')` then `create_client(SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_KEY)` (confirmed in auth.py:11-12, quotes.py:11-12, products.py:10-14, customers.py:10-14, vendors.py:10-14, platform.py:20-22, pdf.py:10-15, ai.py (JWT only, no DB), bom.py:10-18, integrations.py:10-14, projects.py:12-16, proposal.py:19-22).
findings.exploitation_scenario: Not currently exploitable through any code path checked (every route was independently verified to filter by company_id derived from the server-signed JWT). The risk materializes the day a new route, a hotfix, or a refactor omits the filter — there is nothing at the database layer that would catch or block that mistake before it ships.
findings.recommended_remediation: Enable RLS with a `company_id = (auth.jwt() ->> 'company_id')::uuid`-style tenant_isolation policy (same pattern already used in migration-project-performance.sql) on every remaining tenant table: companies, users, invites, quotes, quote_versions, quote_version_reviewers, quote_emails, quote_activity, vendors, products, customers, company_integrations, projects. Because the backend authenticates with its own JWT (not Supabase Auth), `auth.jwt()` will be empty for the service-role connection the app uses in normal operation — RLS becomes a safety net, not a live gate, until/unless the app also adopts Supabase Auth or a lower-privileged key for some paths.
dependencies: Requires a consolidated, versioned migration file since schema.sql itself is stale (see REL-003)
findings.suggested_automated_test: A pgTAP or SQL-script test that connects with the anon/authenticated Supabase role (not service role) and asserts SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE against a foreign company_id row returns zero rows / is denied for every listed table.

findings.title: All three Supabase Storage buckets (product-images, company-assets, proposals) are public with unsigned, non-expiring URLs
findings.business_impact: Any party who obtains a file URL — via browser history, a shared link, a referrer header, a proxy/CDN cache, or by guessing the low-entropy path pattern — can read another company's uploaded logo, product image, or generated technical/commercial proposal PDF (which contains full pricing, BOM, and customer name) with zero authentication.
findings.technical_risk: Paths are namespaced by company_id (e.g. `{company_id}/{pid}-{timestamp}.{ext}`) for organization only, not access control. `get_public_url()` returns a permanent, unauthenticated URL. There is no signed-URL, no expiry, and no server-side check that the requester belongs to the owning company at fetch time.
findings.evidence: api/products.py:395 `public_url = sb.storage.from_(BUCKET).get_public_url(path)`; api/auth.py:764 (company-assets/logo, same pattern); api/proposal.py:713 `url = sb.storage.from_(BUCKET).get_public_url(path)`. No `create_signed_url` call exists anywhere in the codebase (grep-confirmed).
findings.exploitation_scenario: An attacker who sees or intercepts one proposal/logo/product-image URL (e.g. via a shared quote link, a compromised machine's browser history, or a leaky analytics/log pipeline) can fetch that exact file indefinitely with no login. Paths are not sequential/enumerable today (UUID + timestamp), so bulk enumeration is impractical, but this is security-by-obscurity, not access control.
findings.recommended_remediation: Switch product-images, company-assets, and proposals buckets to private. Replace get_public_url() with create_signed_url() (short TTL, e.g. 5-15 minutes), generated per authenticated, company-scoped request at the moment a file is actually displayed/downloaded, rather than persisting a permanent URL in the database.
dependencies: Frontend must be updated to re-request a fresh signed URL rather than caching image_url/logo_url/proposal file URLs indefinitely
findings.suggested_automated_test: Cross-tenant test: fetch a Tenant B file URL with a Tenant A session (or anonymously) and assert 403/404.

findings.title: Live-format Supabase service-role key and JWT secret sit in plaintext in .env.example on disk
findings.resolution_note: Resolved 2026-07-20: the exposed sb_secret_... key belonged to a legacy, already-decommissioned Supabase project (sysconic-quotes / idcvzoqcmgwgqcpnpcuz) that current production/staging traffic does not use (see REL-004 resolution). The user revoked that key directly in the Supabase dashboard (Settings > API Keys > Secret keys), confirmed via screenshot showing 'No secret API keys found'. .env.example and README.md were both updated to remove the real project ref and replace it with an obvious placeholder. The JWT_SECRET value in .env.example was re-examined and found to already be non-functional placeholder text ('pick-a-long-random-string-here-2026'), not a real secret, so no separate JWT_SECRET rotation was required for this finding.
findings.business_impact: If the value is genuinely the live production key (format matches Supabase's current `sb_secret_...` service-role key convention, and the paired SUPABASE_URL matches the project ID recorded in prior project notes), anyone who reads this file has full, RLS-bypassing read/write access to the entire production database.
findings.technical_risk: .env.example is excluded from git by `.gitignore`'s `.env*` rule (confirmed via `git ls-files` — the file is not tracked), so it has not leaked via version control. It is nonetheless sitting as a plaintext value on the local disk in a file whose name and convention ("example") signals it should contain a fake placeholder, not a real secret.
findings.evidence: .env.example line 2 contains a value in the `sb_secret_...` format (value not reproduced in this report); JWT_SECRET is a low-entropy example string rather than a generated secret. Value not reproduced here per audit handling rules.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Any tool, backup process, screen-share, support ticket, or file sync that touches this local file exposes full database access. This includes the fact that this very audit process (an AI agent with file read access) was able to read the value in plaintext.
findings.recommended_remediation: Rotate SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY in the Supabase dashboard immediately, update it in Vercel's encrypted environment variable store for both projects, and replace the value in .env.example with an obviously-fake placeholder (e.g. `sb_secret_xxx_replace_me`). Generate a fresh, high-entropy JWT_SECRET and rotate it too (this will log out every current session platform-wide — acceptable at current scale).
findings.suggested_automated_test: A pre-commit / CI secret-scanning step (gitleaks or trufflehog) that fails the build if any `sb_secret_`, `sb_publishable_`, or high-entropy JWT-secret-shaped string appears in a tracked or staged file.

findings.title: get_version(), list_versions(), and quote_pdf() skip the _can_view_quote() permission check
findings.business_impact: Any authenticated user inside a company can read the full quote_data/terms_data snapshot and reviewer comments of any teammate's private, unshared quote review submission, and can download the finished PDF of any teammate's private quote, bypassing the app's own "only creator / admin / can_view_all_quotes / assigned reviewer" visibility model.
findings.technical_risk: This is a same-company (not cross-tenant) broken object-level authorization gap. All three routes correctly scope the parent quote to `claims['company_id']`, but never call `_can_view_quote()` the way get_quote(), quote_activity(), list_customer_sends(), and get_customer_send() all do.
findings.evidence: api/quotes.py list_versions() (route `/api/quotes/<qid>/versions`, GET) and get_version() (route `/api/quotes/<qid>/versions/<vid>`, GET): both call only `sb.table('quotes').select(...).eq('id', qid).eq('company_id', claims['company_id']).execute()` with no subsequent `_can_view_quote()` call, unlike the sibling routes in the same file. api/pdf.py quote_pdf() (route `/api/pdf/quote/<qid>`, GET): same pattern — company-scoped but not visibility-scoped.
findings.exploitation_scenario: A plain 'user'-role team member who is not the quote's creator, not flagged can_view_all_quotes, and not an assigned reviewer, calls GET /api/quotes/<any-qid-in-their-company>/versions and receives the full version history, including pricing and reviewer comments, for a colleague's private quote — or downloads that colleague's quote as a finished PDF via GET /api/pdf/quote/<qid>.
findings.recommended_remediation: Add `if not _can_view_quote(qid, quote, claims): return jsonify({'error': 'Forbidden'}), 403` to all three routes, matching the pattern already used in get_quote() and quote_activity() in api/quotes.py.
findings.suggested_automated_test: As a non-privileged, non-reviewer teammate, GET another user's quote's /versions and /versions/<vid> and assert 403.

findings.title: JWT stored in localStorage, 30-day expiry, no refresh token, no server-side session revocation
findings.business_impact: A single stored-XSS finding anywhere in the 4,471-line frontend, or a token copied off a compromised/shared machine, remains fully valid for up to 30 days. There is no way to revoke one user's session — the only kill switch is rotating JWT_SECRET, which logs out every user on the entire platform simultaneously.
findings.technical_risk: `make_token()` (api/auth.py:33-41) issues a 30-day HS256 JWT with no `jti`/session-id claim and no server-side token/session table, so there is no mechanism to invalidate a specific token before its natural expiry. The frontend persists it via `localStorage.setItem('sq_token', ...)` (index.html:1097).
findings.evidence: api/auth.py:40 `'exp': datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(days=30)`; index.html:471,1097,1098 (`localStorage.getItem/setItem('sq_token', ...)`, `doLogout()` only calls `localStorage.removeItem`, which does not invalidate the token server-side — a captured token keeps working after the user "logs out" client-side).
findings.exploitation_scenario: An XSS payload (see APP-003) or a stolen browser profile yields a bearer token that remains usable for the full 30-day window even after the legitimate user clicks Logout.
findings.recommended_remediation: Shorten access-token TTL substantially (e.g. 1-24 hours), add a refresh-token flow with a server-side, revocable session/refresh-token table, and make doLogout() call a server endpoint that invalidates the current session server-side rather than only clearing localStorage. At minimum, add a `jti` and a denylist table so a specific compromised token can be revoked without rotating JWT_SECRET for everyone.
findings.suggested_automated_test: Log out, then replay the old bearer token against a protected endpoint and assert it is rejected.

findings.title: No rate limiting or brute-force protection on login, register, forgot-password, or accept-invite
findings.business_impact: Public-facing authentication endpoints can be brute-forced or hammered with no platform-level pushback, risking credential-stuffing account takeover and password-reset-token guessing at scale.
findings.technical_risk: No Flask-Limiter (or equivalent) dependency exists in requirements.txt; no manual attempt-counter, lockout, or CAPTCHA logic exists in api/auth.py's login(), register(), forgot_password(), or accept_invite() routes.
findings.evidence: requirements.txt (no rate-limiting package); api/auth.py login()/register()/forgot_password()/accept_invite() — no throttling logic present in any of them.
findings.exploitation_scenario: An attacker scripts repeated POST /api/auth/login attempts against a known email with a password list; nothing in the application stack slows this down beyond Vercel's own platform-level DDoS protections (not an application control).
findings.recommended_remediation: Add IP- and account-based rate limiting (Flask-Limiter backed by a shared store such as Upstash Redis, since Vercel functions are stateless) to login, register, forgot-password, and accept-invite. Add exponential backoff or temporary lockout after repeated failures on a single account.
dependencies: A shared rate-limit store reachable from serverless functions (Redis/Upstash)
findings.suggested_automated_test: Script N rapid failed logins against one account and assert the platform starts rejecting/delaying before N+1.

findings.title: CORS is wide open (allow-all origins) on every backend route file
findings.business_impact: Any website can issue authenticated cross-origin requests against the API on behalf of a user if it can otherwise obtain that user's bearer token (e.g. via XSS elsewhere), and the wide-open policy simplifies reconnaissance/abuse of the public API surface generally.
findings.technical_risk: api/auth.py explicitly sets `CORS(app, resources={r'/api/*': {'origins': '*'}})`; every other route file uses bare `CORS(app)`, which is Flask-CORS's default allow-all-origins behavior. Because auth uses a Bearer token in an Authorization header (not a cookie), classic CSRF is largely mitigated, but this still removes a real layer of defense-in-depth and is compounded by APP-004 (flask-cors has multiple known CORS-handling CVEs at the pinned version).
findings.evidence: api/auth.py:9 `CORS(app, resources={r"/api/*": {"origins": "*"}})`; api/quotes.py:9, api/products.py:8, api/customers.py:8, api/vendors.py:8, api/platform.py:18, api/pdf.py:8, api/ai.py:7, api/bom.py:8, api/integrations.py:8, api/projects.py:10, api/proposal.py:17 — all bare `CORS(app)`.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Combined with an XSS finding on another site or a browser extension that can read the token from localStorage cross-site, a malicious page could make authenticated calls to the API using a victim's token.
findings.recommended_remediation: Restrict CORS to the app's own known origins (production + staging Vercel domains, plus localhost for dev) via Flask-CORS's `origins` list, rather than the default wildcard.
findings.suggested_automated_test: A cross-origin fetch from a disallowed origin against a protected endpoint should be blocked by the browser's CORS enforcement (verify the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header is not `*` and not the test origin).

findings.title: 19 known vulnerabilities across pinned dependency versions (pip-audit)
findings.business_impact: The application ships with outdated, vulnerable versions of Flask, Flask-CORS, PyJWT, python-dotenv, and requests. Several PyJWT and Flask-CORS advisories are directly relevant given the app's own JWT-based auth and wide-open CORS configuration (API-001).
findings.technical_risk: pip-audit run against the exact pins in requirements.txt (2026-07-20) reported: flask 3.0.3 (1 advisory, fix 3.1.3), flask-cors 4.0.1 (4 advisories, fix 4.0.2/6.0.0), pyjwt 2.8.0 (multiple advisories, fix 2.12.0/2.13.0), python-dotenv 1.0.1 (1 advisory, fix 1.2.2), requests 2.32.3 (2 advisories, fix 2.32.4/2.33.0). Exact CVE/GHSA IDs and severity should be reviewed directly in the pip-audit output (PYSEC identifiers) before prioritizing individual fixes, since not all advisories affect this app's actual usage pattern.
findings.evidence: `pip-audit -r requirements.txt` output, run in this audit session against the pinned versions in requirements.txt.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Varies per advisory; several PyJWT advisories historically relate to algorithm-confusion or decoding edge cases relevant to any app that decodes attacker-supplied tokens, which this app does in verify_token() on every request.
findings.recommended_remediation: Bump flask, flask-cors, pyjwt, python-dotenv, and requests to the patched versions identified by pip-audit; re-run the full test suite and a manual smoke test after the bump (Flask 3.0→3.1 and PyJWT 2.8→2.13 may include behavior changes worth a changelog review).
findings.suggested_automated_test: Add `pip-audit` as a required CI step (see REL-006) so this regresses automatically if pins drift again.

findings.title: Third-party integration credentials (Zoho client_secret / refresh_token) stored in plaintext JSONB, not encrypted at rest
findings.business_impact: A refresh_token grants long-lived, renewable access to a customer's own Zoho Books accounting data. Storing it as plaintext JSON means anyone with database access (service-role key holder, a DB backup, a misconfigured admin tool) can read every connected customer's live accounting-system credentials, not just this app's own data.
findings.technical_risk: connect_integration() (api/integrations.py) upserts `credentials: creds` directly into `company_integrations.credentials` with no application-layer encryption. A `mask()` helper exists but is used only for API response display, not for storage.
findings.evidence: api/integrations.py connect_integration(): `sb.table('company_integrations').upsert({'company_id': ..., 'provider': provider, 'credentials': creds, 'status': 'connected', ...})`; `mask(value)` is called only inside `list_integrations()`'s response building, never before the upsert.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Database exposure (via the .env.example secret in APP-001, an insider, or a future SQL-injection/backup-leak elsewhere) yields working Zoho credentials for every connected tenant, not just quote data.
findings.recommended_remediation: Encrypt the `credentials` column payload at the application layer (e.g. AES-GCM with a key held in Vercel's environment, separate from SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY) before insert, and decrypt only at the point of use inside the Zoho adapter. Consider Supabase Vault if available on the project's plan.
dependencies: A dedicated encryption key in environment config, key-rotation plan
findings.suggested_automated_test: Query the raw `company_integrations.credentials` column directly and assert the value is not valid plaintext JSON/does not contain the known refresh_token substring.

findings.title: Frontend XSS exposure not fully verified across all 78 innerHTML sites
findings.business_impact: If any user-controlled string (quote title, customer name, product description, terms text, AI-drafted proposal content) reaches innerHTML without the app's `esc()` helper, a stored-XSS payload could execute in the context of a company admin's session, and combined with AUTH-002's 30-day non-revocable token, would be highly damaging.
findings.technical_risk: index.html defines and consistently uses an `esc()` helper in the specific locations sampled in this audit (customer name, item description, quote title in the compare/review/print views — index.html:1542,1646,1698,2619,2639,2673,2707,2726,2809,3110,3154). The file contains 78 total innerHTML usages; this audit sampled roughly 20 and found consistent escaping in every one, but did not exhaustively review all 78, nor the AI-drafted proposal content path (content.title/executive_summary/etc. rendered client-side before render_proposal() is called) or the print/PDF HTML-generation path for injection risk.
findings.evidence: index.html: `esc(...)` wraps user data in every sampled innerHTML template-literal site; no counter-example of an unescaped user field found in the sample, but coverage was not exhaustive.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Unverified — would require either finding an unescaped site among the remaining ~58 unreviewed innerHTML usages, or confirming the AI proposal-draft content (which is LLM-generated but seeded with user-controlled project descriptions) is escaped before rendering into the proposal editor UI.
findings.recommended_remediation: Run a dedicated XSS review (manual or via an automated DOM-XSS scanner such as a headless-browser fuzz pass) across all 78 innerHTML sites, with particular attention to the AI-drafted proposal content path and any field rendered inside the print/PDF HTML builder, which is also sent server-side to PDFShift as raw HTML (see API-004).
findings.suggested_automated_test: Set a quote title / customer name / product description to `` and confirm it renders as inert text everywhere it is displayed, including the AI proposal draft and PDF outputs.

findings.title: Server-side HTML-to-PDF rendering (PDFShift) accepts client-submitted HTML with no server-side sanitization
findings.business_impact: email_quote() and render_proposal() forward client-constructed HTML (built by the frontend's own print-view renderer) directly to PDFShift for conversion. If any upstream field feeding that HTML is unescaped (see APP-003), this becomes a second injection surface — HTML/CSS injection into a document later emailed to a real customer under the tenant's name.
findings.technical_risk: api/quotes.py email_quote(): `html = d.get('html') or ''` is taken as-is from the request body and posted to PDFShift's convert API with `use_print: True`. api/pdf.py render_pdf() does the same for the standalone PDF-render endpoint. There is no server-side HTML sanitizer (e.g. bleach) in requirements.txt.
findings.evidence: api/quotes.py email_quote() lines ~977-1006; api/pdf.py render_pdf() lines ~369-401; requirements.txt has no HTML-sanitization library.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Relies on APP-003 (frontend escaping) holding everywhere; if it doesn't, injected content could alter the PDF a customer receives (e.g. false pricing/terms rendered as legitimate-looking text, or exfiltration via CSS/external resource loading during PDFShift's render).
findings.recommended_remediation: Treat the HTML payload as untrusted at the API boundary even though it originates from the app's own frontend: sanitize/allowlist tags server-side before forwarding to PDFShift, and disable external resource loading in the PDFShift render options if supported.
dependencies: Resolves cleanly once APP-003 is closed, but should be a defense-in-depth layer regardless
findings.suggested_automated_test: Submit an html payload containing a script/style-based exfil attempt to /api/pdf/render and confirm it is neutralized in the output PDF.

findings.title: An awarded quote's live commercial content can be reverted to draft and edited without re-approval, after the Project Performance baseline has already frozen a snapshot
findings.business_impact: The one durable, tamper-evident commercial snapshot of an awarded deal (`project_commercial_baselines`) only exists if the Project Performance feature is enabled and the "Create Project" action was taken. Otherwise, an awarded quote can be set back to status='draft' (update_quote() explicitly allows editing once status is 'draft' again) and its quote_data edited with no new approval cycle and no automatic record of what changed.
findings.technical_risk: update_quote() (api/quotes.py) only blocks edits when `old_status != 'draft' and not is_transitioning and touches_content`; transitioning the status back to 'draft' is itself an allowed update, after which content edits are unblocked. quote_activity logs the status transition itself but does not diff/store the before/after quote_data on a subsequent content edit.
findings.evidence: api/quotes.py update_quote(): the 423 lock only fires for the non-transition, content-touching case; a two-step call (1: set status→draft, 2: edit quote_data) bypasses it entirely and is logged only as a generic 'status_changed' activity entry, not as a content change with a diff.
findings.exploitation_scenario: A well-intentioned but undisciplined user reopens an awarded quote to "fix a typo," inadvertently changing pricing after the customer has already signed off, with no forced re-approval and no diff trail beyond the generic status-change log line.
findings.recommended_remediation: Require an explicit reason and (for admin-only) a distinct "reopen awarded quote" action separate from the generic status field update; snapshot quote_data into quote_versions (or a new immutable revisions table) automatically whenever an awarded/sent quote is reopened, regardless of whether Project Performance is enabled.
dependencies: Could reuse the existing quote_versions table/pattern
findings.suggested_automated_test: Award a quote, revert to draft, edit quote_data, and assert a full pre-edit snapshot exists and is retrievable.

findings.title: Monetary calculations use IEEE-754 floating point (Python float / JS Number), duplicated across four independent implementations
findings.business_impact: Floating-point arithmetic is not exact for decimal currency math; combined with the pricing formula being hand-duplicated in four places, there is both a rounding-drift risk and a maintenance risk where a formula fix applied in one file silently fails to propagate to the others.
findings.technical_risk: calc_item()/calc_opt() (or _calc_item_pp()) are implemented independently in api/pdf.py, api/proposal.py, api/quotes.py (Project Performance baseline calc), and again in index.html's client-side JS — a Vercel one-file-per-route constraint forces this duplication (documented in code comments) but nothing enforces the four copies stay in sync.
findings.evidence: api/pdf.py calc_item()/calc_opt(); api/proposal.py calc_item()/calc_opt() (near-identical); api/quotes.py _calc_item_pp(); index.html's own calcItem()/calcOpt() referenced by tests/run-tests.mjs. All use Python `float`/`round()` or JS `Number`/`Math.round()`, not a fixed-point/decimal type.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Not an attacker-exploitable bug; a data-integrity/accuracy risk. A formula change (e.g. a rounding-mode fix) applied to index.html's calcItem() but missed in api/pdf.py's calc_item() would make the PDF total silently disagree with the on-screen total.
findings.recommended_remediation: Consolidate the pricing formula into one place if the Vercel function-count/import constraint can be worked around (e.g. a shared internal HTTP micro-endpoint, or moving off the one-file-per-route Vercel Python builder to a framework that supports shared modules), and use integer minor-units or Python's Decimal for all monetary math. Short of a full consolidation, add the automated cross-file parity test described in TEST-004.
dependencies: Architectural decision on how to share code across Vercel Python functions (see PROPOSED-TARGET-ARCHITECTURE.md)
findings.suggested_automated_test: Golden-value test: run the same fixed line-item input through every one of the four implementations and assert identical output to the cent.

findings.title: schema.sql and migration files do not represent the actual live database schema
findings.business_impact: There is no reliable, versioned single source of truth for the database schema. New engineers (or an AI agent) reading schema.sql would miss the existence of customers, company_integrations, and projects tables entirely, and would materially misjudge tenant-column coverage and constraints on those tables.
findings.technical_risk: grep across every *.sql file in the repo finds no `CREATE TABLE` statement for `customers`, `company_integrations`, or `projects`, despite all three being actively read/written by deployed routes (api/customers.py, api/integrations.py, api/projects.py). schema.sql's own comments acknowledge this pattern already happened once for vendors/products ("was previously only created via an earlier, untracked migration").
findings.evidence: `grep -n "create table" *.sql` output lists only companies/users/invites/quotes/quote_versions/quote_version_reviewers/quote_emails/quote_activity/vendors/products (schema.sql) plus the 21 Project Performance tables (migration-project-performance.sql) — customers/company_integrations/projects are absent from every tracked .sql file.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Not an attack vector; an operational/reliability risk — RLS/constraint/index work planned off schema.sql alone (as this very audit had to guard against) will silently miss these three tables.
findings.recommended_remediation: Reverse-engineer the current live schema directly from Supabase (via the dashboard's schema export or `pg_dump --schema-only`) and commit it as the new baseline, then adopt a strict "every schema change ships as a numbered migration file, no manual dashboard DDL" policy going forward, ideally enforced by a migration tool (Supabase CLI migrations, or Alembic-style versioning).
findings.suggested_automated_test: A CI check that diffs the committed schema.sql/migrations against a live schema dump and fails on drift.

findings.title: Two orphaned backend route files (api/pp_sync.py, api/project_performance.py) exist in the repo but are not registered in vercel.json
findings.business_impact: Dead code that duplicates logic now living in api/projects.py (per its own header comment) creates confusion risk and a repeat of a previously-fixed incident: api/zoho.py was flagged as exactly this kind of orphaned, unreachable, stale-schema-assuming file in a prior audit and was subsequently deleted. If pp_sync.py/project_performance.py are ever accidentally re-registered (e.g. during a vercel.json merge conflict resolution), they would run against a schema/logic snapshot that has since diverged from projects.py.
findings.technical_risk: vercel.json's `builds`/`routes` arrays list exactly 12 Python files (the Vercel Hobby plan's Serverless Function cap, per comments in projects.py); pp_sync.py and project_performance.py are not among them.
findings.evidence: vercel.json builds array (12 entries, no pp_sync.py/project_performance.py); api/projects.py header comment: "Project Performance — originally api/project_performance.py and api/pp_sync.py, merged in here because Vercel's Hobby plan caps a deployment at 12 Serverless Functions".
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A — code hygiene / operational risk, not directly exploitable.
findings.recommended_remediation: Delete api/pp_sync.py and api/project_performance.py from the repository (their logic already lives, maintained, inside api/projects.py).
findings.suggested_automated_test: A CI lint step asserting every file under api/*.py is referenced in vercel.json's builds array (or is explicitly allowlisted as intentionally unregistered).

findings.title: No structured logging or error monitoring; errors go to print()/traceback only
findings.business_impact: A broken feature in production (e.g. the previously-encountered password-reset email bug, referenced in project notes) can go unnoticed until a user reports it, with no proactive alerting.
findings.technical_risk: Error handling throughout api/*.py is `traceback.print_exc()` plus a JSON error response; this is only visible by someone actively checking Vercel's function logs. No Sentry, Logtail, Datadog, or equivalent APM/error-tracking integration exists in requirements.txt or anywhere in the codebase.
findings.evidence: requirements.txt has no logging/APM package; every api/*.py file's exception handling uses bare `print()`/`traceback.print_exc()`.
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A — operational risk.
findings.recommended_remediation: Add a lightweight error-monitoring SDK (Sentry has a lightweight Flask/serverless-friendly integration) and route all exception handlers through it; include company_id and user_id (not full quote content) as structured tags for correlation, per OBS-002.
findings.suggested_automated_test: Trigger a deliberate exception in a staging deploy and confirm it appears in the monitoring dashboard within the expected latency.

findings.title: No platform-admin audit log for suspend/reactivate company, create company, create platform admin, or invite-to-company
findings.business_impact: Zero forensic trail exists for the most privileged actions on the platform. If a platform-admin account is compromised or misused, there is no record of what it did.
findings.technical_risk: api/platform.py's suspend_company(), reactivate_company(), create_company(), create_platform_admin(), and invite_to_company() perform their database writes directly with no corresponding insert into any audit/event table (no such table exists in schema.sql or any migration).
findings.evidence: api/platform.py — every mutating route (suspend_company:207-213, reactivate_company:215-221, create_company:163-204, invite_to_company:230-274, create_platform_admin:280-311) contains no audit-log write.
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A directly, but materially weakens incident response: a rogue or compromised platform-admin session could suspend a competitor's tenant, or mint additional platform-admin accounts, with no record of who did it or when.
findings.recommended_remediation: Add a `platform_audit_log` table (actor_id, action, target_company_id, detail, ip_address, user_agent, created_at) and insert a row from every route in api/platform.py; extend the same pattern to company-level admin actions (role changes, invites) per OBS-002.
findings.suggested_automated_test: Call each platform.py mutating route and assert a corresponding audit_log row is created with the correct actor/action/target.

findings.title: Company-level audit trail (quote_activity) does not capture IP address, user agent, or before/after values for financially significant edits
findings.business_impact: quote_activity provides a readable action timeline (created, status_changed, submitted_for_review, admin_force_approved, emailed_to_customer, etc.) but does not record the old/new value for what actually changed, nor the actor's IP/user agent, limiting its usefulness as a compliance-grade audit log.
findings.technical_risk: quote_activity (schema.sql:163-171) has columns quote_id, action, detail (free text), actor_id, created_at only — no before_value/after_value/ip_address/user_agent/correlation_id columns.
findings.evidence: schema.sql:163-171 create table quote_activity; _log_activity() in api/quotes.py inserts only {quote_id, actor_id, action, detail}.
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A — compliance/forensics gap, not directly exploitable.
findings.recommended_remediation: Add ip_address, user_agent, and structured before_value/after_value JSONB columns to quote_activity (or a new generalized audit_log table covering non-quote entities too — customers, products, team/role changes), and start recording the request's originating IP (available via Vercel's forwarded headers) and diffed field values on every write.
findings.suggested_automated_test: Perform a price change on a quote and assert the resulting activity/audit row contains the old and new total_sell values.

findings.title: No backend (Python/API) automated tests exist; only a frontend jsdom test suite
findings.business_impact: None of the tenant-isolation, authorization, pricing-parity-across-files, RLS, or Zoho integration logic living in api/*.py has any automated regression coverage. Confidence in "no cross-tenant leak" rests entirely on manual code review (this audit and the two prior ones), not on a test suite that runs on every commit.
findings.technical_risk: tests/ contains a single file, run-tests.mjs, which boots index.html in jsdom and tests frontend pricing math, typing-persistence regressions, and print-layout rendering with a mocked fetch — it never calls the real Flask backend or a real/test Supabase instance. .github/workflows/tests.yml only runs this one frontend suite on push/PR.
findings.evidence: tests/ directory listing: run-tests.mjs only; .github/workflows/tests.yml: single job `frontend-tests` running `node tests/run-tests.mjs`.
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A — coverage gap.
findings.recommended_remediation: Add a Python test suite (pytest) that exercises each api/*.py Flask app directly against a disposable/test Supabase project (or a mocked Supabase client), covering at minimum: tenant isolation (TEN-001's suggested test), the AUTH-001 permission gap, pricing-formula parity across files (QUO-002), and the full auth lifecycle (register/login/invite/reset). Wire it into .github/workflows/tests.yml as a second required job.
dependencies: A dedicated test Supabase project/schema, isolated from staging and production (also needed to fix REL-004)
findings.suggested_automated_test: This finding IS the recommendation — see TESTING-GAP-ANALYSIS.md for the full minimum regression suite.

findings.title: Staging environment has historically shared the production Supabase database (status at time of last internal check: unresolved)
findings.resolution_note: Resolved and confirmed 2026-07-20 during remediation: production Vercel project (sysconic-quotes) SUPABASE_URL confirmed pointing to the sysconic-quotes-prod Supabase project (aekgviydbagyllutafuz); staging Vercel project (sysconic-quotes-staging) SUPABASE_URL confirmed pointing to the separate sysconic-quotes-staging Supabase project (rvnvjirlxxngqlnlavii). Verified directly against the Vercel dashboard by the user, not inferred from repo files. The original .env.example/.env.local also referenced a third, now-decommissioned legacy Supabase project (sysconic-quotes, idcvzoqcmgwgqcpnpcuz) which has been confirmed unused and had its exposed secret key revoked as part of closing APP-001.
findings.business_impact: If staging and production still point at the same Supabase project, any test/dev activity on staging (including load-testing the new automated test suite recommended in TEST-001) writes directly into production data, and staging bugs can corrupt real customer data.
findings.technical_risk: This was flagged as an open, unresolved item in project notes as of this audit's start ("Separate staging Supabase database ... until then staging shares prod DB; test quotes must be prefixed or deleted"). This audit had no access to the Vercel dashboard's environment-variable configuration for either project and could not independently confirm whether SUPABASE_URL differs between the `sysconic-quotes` and `sysconic-quotes-staging` Vercel projects.
findings.evidence: Prior session notes describing this as a pending action item; api/auth.py's own `get_app_url()` function was specifically rewritten (per its docstring) to stop a related staging/production URL cross-link bug, which corroborates that environment separation has been an active, recurring problem area in this project.
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A directly — an operational data-integrity risk rather than a security exploit.
findings.recommended_remediation: Confirm in the Vercel dashboard whether both projects' SUPABASE_URL values differ; if not, provision a separate Supabase project for staging, migrate the schema (schema.sql plus all migration-*.sql files, corrected per REL-001), and repoint staging's environment variables.
dependencies: REL-001 (schema.sql must be accurate before it can be replayed onto a fresh staging database)
findings.suggested_automated_test: A CI/deploy-time assertion that staging's SUPABASE_URL differs from production's.

findings.title: No subscription/plan/usage-limit enforcement beyond free-text plan and status columns
findings.business_impact: The platform cannot yet meter or cap usage (users, quotes, storage, AI calls, PDF generations, email volume) per company, and has no trial-expiry, grace-period, or billing-webhook plumbing — it is not ready to sell metered or tiered plans.
findings.technical_risk: companies.plan and companies.status (schema.sql:6-7) are free-text with no accompanying trial_start/trial_end/max_users/quota columns, no entitlements table, and no billing-provider webhook endpoint anywhere in api/*.py or vercel.json's routes.
findings.evidence: schema.sql:2-14 companies table definition; grep across api/*.py finds no Stripe/Chargebee/Paddle SDK, no webhook route matching a billing provider's callback shape, and no `features`/`limits` enforcement beyond the ad hoc `companies.features` JSONB used solely to gate the Project Performance module (`_has_feature`/`has_feature` checks in api/quotes.py and api/projects.py).
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A — product/business readiness gap, not a security exploit; though note that the existing `features` JSONB flag IS read from the JWT claims (`claims.get('features')`) rather than re-checked against the live companies row on every request, meaning a feature disabled after token issuance stays enabled in that user's session for up to 30 days (AUTH-002 compounds this).
findings.recommended_remediation: Design and add a proper entitlements model (plans table, company_subscriptions table with status/trial_end/current_period_end, and a usage_counters table) before any paid tiering goes live; re-check feature flags server-side against the live company row rather than trusting the JWT snapshot, or shorten token TTL so drift is bounded.
dependencies: A chosen billing provider (Stripe is the de facto standard for this scale) and its webhook idempotency handling
findings.suggested_automated_test: Toggle a company's plan/feature server-side and assert an already-issued token loses/gains access within a bounded time window rather than up to 30 days.

findings.title: No documented subprocessor inventory, data-retention policy, or tenant-offboarding/export workflow
findings.business_impact: The app already sends tenant business data to four external subprocessors (Supabase for storage/DB, Microsoft Graph for email, Google Gemini for AI features, Brave Search and PDFShift for image/PDF services) with no published subprocessor list, no documented retention period, and no self-service or admin-triggered tenant data export/deletion endpoint.
findings.technical_risk: No `/api/*/export` or account-deletion route exists anywhere in api/*.py; no data-retention logic (e.g. auto-purging old password_resets, quote_emails, or activity rows) was found.
findings.evidence: Cross-referenced against the full route inventory in API-SECURITY-AUDIT.md — no export/deletion endpoints exist; Gemini (api/ai.py, api/bom.py, api/proposal.py), Microsoft Graph (api/auth.py, api/quotes.py), Brave Search (api/products.py), and PDFShift (api/pdf.py, api/quotes.py) are all confirmed live external data recipients.
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A — compliance readiness gap.
findings.recommended_remediation: Publish a subprocessor list, define retention periods per table, and add both a platform-admin-triggered and (eventually) self-service tenant data export (JSON/CSV dump of a company's own data) and a documented tenant-deletion workflow (soft-delete with a grace period, then hard purge across all tenant-owned tables and storage paths).
findings.suggested_automated_test: Trigger a tenant export and assert it contains exactly that company's rows across every tenant-owned table, with none from any other company.

findings.title: Company-scoped feature flags and role are baked into the JWT at login rather than re-checked live
findings.business_impact: Demoting a user's role, revoking can_view_all_quotes/can_review, or disabling a company feature takes effect only after that user's token expires or they log in again (up to 30 days later given AUTH-002), not immediately.
findings.technical_risk: make_token() embeds `role`, `is_platform_admin`, and `features` at issuance; most authorization checks in api/*.py read `claims['role']`/`claims.get('features')` directly from the decoded token rather than re-querying the live users/companies row (the one documented exception is `_can_view_all_quotes()` in api/quotes.py, which explicitly re-queries live to avoid this exact staleness for that one flag).
findings.evidence: api/auth.py make_token():33-41; api/quotes.py `_can_view_all_quotes()` docstring explicitly calls out that it re-queries live "so toggling the flag takes effect without forcing a re-login" — implying every other claim (role, features, is_platform_admin) does not get this treatment.
findings.exploitation_scenario: A company admin demotes a user mid-session; that user's existing token still carries role='admin' and continues to pass every `claims['role'] != 'admin'` check for up to 30 days.
findings.recommended_remediation: Either shorten token TTL substantially (ties into AUTH-002's broader fix) or move to re-checking role/is_platform_admin/features live per request (with caching) the same way `_can_view_all_quotes()` already does, accepting the extra DB round-trip.
findings.suggested_automated_test: Demote a user's role server-side mid-session and assert their existing token loses admin-only access within the target window.

findings.title: Inconsistent global error handling across route files — some leak raw Flask HTML 500 pages instead of JSON
findings.business_impact: An unhandled exception in a file without a global `@app.errorhandler(Exception)` (api/quotes.py, api/auth.py, api/platform.py, api/pdf.py, api/ai.py, api/bom.py) returns Flask's default HTML error page instead of the JSON shape the frontend expects, breaking the UI's error handling and potentially leaking a stack trace to the client depending on Flask debug settings.
findings.technical_risk: api/products.py, api/customers.py, api/vendors.py, api/integrations.py, api/projects.py register a global `@app.errorhandler(Exception)` that normalizes any uncaught exception to JSON; api/quotes.py, api/auth.py, api/platform.py, api/pdf.py, api/ai.py, api/bom.py, api/proposal.py rely only on route-level try/except (auth.py, platform.py) or nothing at all (quotes.py, pdf.py, ai.py, bom.py, proposal.py) for the same protection.
findings.evidence: Direct comparison of the `@app.errorhandler` presence across all 12 deployed api/*.py files read in this audit.
findings.exploitation_scenario: An attacker sending a malformed request that triggers an unhandled exception in one of these files gets Flask's default error page rather than a clean JSON error, which is more likely to reveal implementation details.
findings.recommended_remediation: Add the same `@app.errorhandler(Exception)` pattern already used in products.py/customers.py/vendors.py/integrations.py/projects.py to the remaining files, and confirm `app.run(debug=True)` in every file's `if __name__ == '__main__'` block is never reachable in the Vercel production runtime (it is only used for local dev, but worth an explicit confirmation).
findings.suggested_automated_test: Send a malformed JSON body to each route and assert every response is valid JSON with an 'error' key, never an HTML page.

findings.title: remove_image() never deletes the underlying storage object
findings.business_impact: Orphaned files accumulate indefinitely in the (currently public — TEN-002) product-images bucket, growing storage cost and leaving stale files reachable by anyone who has ever seen their URL, even after a user believes they've removed the image.
findings.technical_risk: api/products.py remove_image() only nulls the `products.image_url` column; it never calls `sb.storage.from_(BUCKET).remove([path])`.
findings.evidence: api/products.py remove_image() route body: `sb.table('products').update({'image_url': None, ...}).eq('id', pid).execute()` — no storage.remove call.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Compounds TEN-002: a "removed" image remains publicly fetchable forever at its original signed/public URL.
findings.recommended_remediation: Call `sb.storage.from_(BUCKET).remove([old_path])` (parsed from the existing image_url) before/after nulling the column.
findings.suggested_automated_test: Remove a product image and assert the storage object no longer exists (404 on fetch).

findings.title: CI runs only the frontend jsdom suite; no lint, type-check, dependency-audit, secret-scan, or backend test gate exists before merge to staging/main
findings.business_impact: Code can reach the `staging` and `main` branches (which auto-deploy per project notes) with no automated check beyond the one existing frontend test file — no Python linting, no dependency vulnerability scan, no secret-scanning, and no backend tests of any kind gate a merge.
findings.technical_risk: .github/workflows/tests.yml defines exactly one job (`frontend-tests`) running `node tests/run-tests.mjs`. There is no second job for `pip-audit`/`ruff`/`flake8`/`mypy`/`bandit`/`gitleaks`.
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/tests.yml full contents: single job, single step beyond checkout/setup-node.
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A — process gap that allowed several of this report's other findings (e.g. APP-001's secret, APP-004's outdated dependencies) to persist undetected.
findings.recommended_remediation: Add CI jobs for: Python lint (ruff/flake8), pip-audit, a secret scanner (gitleaks), and once TEST-001 exists, the backend pytest suite — all required checks before merge to staging/main.
findings.suggested_automated_test: This finding IS the recommendation.

findings.title: No security response headers configured (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy)
findings.business_impact: Without an explicit Content-Security-Policy and frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options protection, the app has one less layer of defense against XSS impact (APP-003) and is not protected against clickjacking via iframe embedding.
findings.technical_risk: vercel.json defines only version/builds/routes/crons — no headers array. Vercel may apply some platform defaults, but this was not verified against a live response and should not be assumed.
findings.evidence: vercel.json full contents reviewed — no `headers` key present.
findings.exploitation_scenario: A malicious site iframes the app (clickjacking) or, combined with an XSS finding, a missing CSP removes a layer that could otherwise have blocked the injected script from executing or exfiltrating data.
findings.recommended_remediation: Add a `headers` array to vercel.json applying Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY (or CSP frame-ancestors 'none'), Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, and Strict-Transport-Security to all routes.
findings.suggested_automated_test: Fetch the deployed app and assert each expected header is present with the expected value.

findings.title: api/platform.py's list_companies() loads every users and quotes row platform-wide into Python memory to compute per-company counts
findings.business_impact: Fine at current scale; becomes a real latency and memory problem as the number of companies/users/quotes grows, since this single admin-panel page load pulls full table scans of users and quotes with no aggregation pushed to the database.
findings.technical_risk: list_companies() (api/platform.py:134-160) does `sb.table('users').select('id,company_id').execute()` and `sb.table('quotes').select('id,company_id').execute()` unbounded, then counts in a Python loop.
findings.evidence: api/platform.py:141-142 (unbounded selects), 144-149 (Python-side counting loop).
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A — scalability risk, not a security exploit; though an unbounded, unauthenticated-adjacent (platform-admin-only, but still) full-table read is worth noting as a resource-consumption concern ("unrestricted resource consumption" per the API security checklist) if the platform-admin token itself is ever compromised.
findings.recommended_remediation: Replace with a single aggregation query (`select company_id, count(*)` grouped) or a materialized view refreshed periodically, rather than loading full tables into the function's memory.
findings.suggested_automated_test: Load-test list_companies() with a synthetic dataset of 10,000 users/quotes and assert response time stays within an acceptable bound.

findings.title: No pagination on several list endpoints; several routes fetch unbounded row sets
findings.business_impact: products/customers/vendors already support limit/offset (capped at 100/1000 respectively). quotes.py's list_quotes() supports limit/offset (default 500, capped 1000) — this is actually implemented, contrary to the older internal audit's note that it was missing; verified current as of this pass. However, list_versions(), quote_activity(), list_customer_sends(), and the Project Performance detail sub-resources (purchase_orders/bills/expenses/invoices/payments/snapshots/alerts inside pp_project_detail()) all fetch full, unbounded result sets per call.
findings.technical_risk: pp_project_detail() (api/projects.py) issues roughly a dozen unbounded `.select('*').eq('project_id', pid).execute()` calls per page load; on a long-lived project with years of Zoho transaction history this will grow unbounded.
findings.evidence: api/projects.py pp_project_detail(): pos/bills/expenses/invoices/payments/forecasts/progress/budget_revisions/snapshots/alerts are all fetched with no limit/offset.
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A — scalability risk.
findings.recommended_remediation: Add pagination (or a sensible hard cap plus a "load more") to the Project Performance detail sub-resource queries and to quote_activity/list_versions/list_customer_sends, prioritized by whichever grows fastest in practice (invoices/bills for long-running projects).
findings.suggested_automated_test: Seed a project with >1,000 synthetic bill rows and assert pp_project_detail() response time/payload size stays bounded.

findings.title: No idempotency keys on financially/operationally significant POST endpoints (Zoho project creation, quote email send)
findings.business_impact: A double-click or client retry on "Create Project" or "Email to customer" risks a duplicate downstream side effect (a second Zoho project, or the customer receiving the same quote email twice), though several routes already have partial, ad hoc idempotency guards.
findings.technical_risk: zoho_create_project() (api/integrations.py) checks `if proj.get('zoho_project_id'): return 409` — a reasonable idempotency guard, but keyed on application state rather than a client-supplied idempotency key, so a race between two near-simultaneous requests before the first write lands is still possible. email_quote() has no duplicate-send guard at all beyond normal user behavior.
findings.evidence: api/integrations.py zoho_create_project() 409 check; api/quotes.py email_quote() — no equivalent guard.
findings.exploitation_scenario: N/A — reliability/UX risk more than a security one, though duplicate customer-facing emails are a real business/reputation cost.
findings.recommended_remediation: Add a short-lived, client-generated idempotency-key header pattern (store recently-seen keys per company for a bounded window) on email_quote() and other customer-facing send actions; keep the existing application-state check on zoho_create_project() but consider a DB-level unique constraint as a stronger backstop.
findings.suggested_automated_test: Fire two concurrent identical email_quote() requests and assert only one customer email is actually sent.
